messages.author: df2ff87426a98fc9
messages.subject: Species as Fixed Effect
parts:
Hello Group,

I have avian point-count data collected using a dependent double-observer method and wish to test competing hypotheses between groups of species (similar to DeWan et al 2009) using gmultmix. Species are grouped a priori into different guilds based on clutch initiation date and diet:

Site     Species     Obs1     Obs2    CID        Diet
1         X               4           0          Y            Y
1         Y               1           1          N            Y
1         Z                0          0          Y            N
2         Y               3           2          N            Y
...

My question is, is it possible to do this in unmarked and if so, how should the data be structure? For example, I know you cannot do multi-species analyses, so how do you take the above example that has multiple rows of data per site and transform it into the appropriate data frame (again, as in DeWan et al 2009).

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Species as Fixed Effect
parts:
Species becomes a site-specific covariate, so your new "sites" in the data frame are a combination of the original site and species (e.g., 1X, 1Y, 2Y).

In the multi-species analysis where species is treated as a random effect (typically using WinBUGS), each parameter has a species-specific estimate.  Essentially, that is the same as specifying that each parameter has an interaction with species.  So for your model, you would want each site covariate to interact with species, unless you had a plausible reason for thinking the effect of the covariate was common to all species.

The problem with having each site covariate interact with a fixed effect for species is that you don't really gain anything from the multi-species analysis over running separate models for each species individually, especially if you know how to run for-loops in R.  The multi-species models which treat species as a random effect benefit from estimating fewer parameters and sharing information across species.

-Dan

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Species as Fixed Effect
parts: That's a good point, Marc.  I suppose model selection is made easier with the multi-species construction.  But model selection won't tell you which species are strongly associated with a given site covariate, only whether all species are or are not equal in their association.  And formal pairwise tests would require some multiple comparison correction.  Depending on the number of species, the interpretation of output can become a bit muddled and overwhelming.

messages.author: 6a288128bce8283d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Species as Fixed Effect
parts:
Hi Dan R.,

In a paper that was just published yesterday
(http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2012.07681.x/abstract)
we opted against grouping species a priori as we compared DeWan et al.
2009's approach and individual species models and found that for a
'forest-reliant' species group (identified by expert birders) yielded
not enough model overlap to justify pooling species. This is why we
initially modelled each species response individually and later pooled
averaged predictions using weights created by expert scores.
The R-code used to generate model lists is in the online supplementary
material and you would of course be welcome to recent updates to this
code if you are interested.

For the paper we used unmarked and we are currently working on adopting
(at least parts) for use in WinBUGS.

Cheers,
Richard S

I am trying to estimate total duck abundance in relation to habitat use and am not concerned with species-specific estimates at this point. Thus, in order to reduce the complexity I thought that grouping species would be a reasonable method.

There are biological and systematic reasons that would suggest some species have similar detection probabilities (e.g., dabbling vs diving ducks), plus the data for some species is sparse so grouping them with other, more common species would allow us to improve estimates. Also, as Marc mentioned, I want to formally test different hypotheses about habitat use between groups, thus I have different guild groupings.

I am having difficulty conceptualizing how this should work, but if I understand correctly, my dataset should look like this:

Site-Species    Obs1       Obs2        Species         GuildA         GuildB

001-X               1              0                X               Dabbler        Large

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Species as Fixed Effect
parts:
Your definition of site should be a unique combination of location (original site ID) and whichever species group covariates you decide to include.  Each record should be "site-GuildA-GuildB" and the counts for Obs1 and Obs2 should be all individuals at the site that fit GuildA and GuildB.

For example, if species X and species V are both Large Dabblers, then their counts should be combined for a given site.  Your data snippet works but it gives the impression that each species already has a unique GuildA-GuildB combination.
